title: A Case of Primary Central Nervous System Lymphoma Mimic Neuromyelitis Optica
case_prompt: A 47-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of neck pain, 2 days of shoulder pain, right-sided chest numbness, and weakness of the upper limbs. He denied weight loss, hypertension, diabetes, smoking, or alcohol use. Neurological examination showed mild left facial weakness, hypoaesthesia below T4 on the right, normal muscle tone, upper-limb strength 4–/5, lower-limb strength 5/5, normal tendon reflexes, negative Kernig’s and Brudzinski’s signs, positive bilateral Babinski signs, and a left Hoffmann sign. Tests for viral antibodies, syphilis serology, and HIV antibodies were negative. Lumbar puncture revealed normal opening pressure; CSF had 10 red cells/µL, 220 nuclear cells/µL, protein 91 mg/dL, normal chloride and glucose, no oligoclonal bands, and no tumor cells. Flow cytometry of CSF showed no abnormal cell differentiation. Serum antinuclear antibodies, extractable nuclear antigen, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were all negative. Serum cytokines showed slightly elevated IL-6 and TNF-α; IL-2, IL-10, IL-17, and IFN-γ were normal. Serum anti-AQP4 antibodies were positive at a titer of 1:10. MRI of the cervical spinal cord revealed multiple T2-hyperintense, enhancing lesions from C2 to T1 with cord enlargement and brain-stem involvement. Brain MRI showed FLAIR hyperintensities in the bilateral thalami, periventricular regions, basal ganglia, and cerebral peduncles. The working diagnosis was neuromyelitis optica, and the patient received high-dose methylprednisolone and immunoglobulin, with progressive symptomatic improvement.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Neuromyelitis optica was the initial diagnosis because “Combination of the clinical symptoms, neurological examination, laboratory examination and magnetic resonance imaging … was consistent with the diagnosis of NMO.”  
2. Paraneoplastic antibody response was considered since “NMO-IgG possibly being a paraneoplastic marker” and AQP4 seropositivity can arise from tumor antigen expression.  
3. Primary central nervous system lymphoma became likely when “MRS showed a high resonance of free lipids and Cho/NAA ratio (4.8-5.1) … which was in favor of a tumoral process.”  
4. PET imaging supported lymphoma with “obviously increased 18-Fludeoxyglucose uptake … the maximum SUV value is 23.6, indicating PCNSL possible.”  
5. Biopsy confirmed the diagnosis as “non-Hodgkin malignant B-cell lymphoma” on immunohistochemical analysis.
